paragraphs: Adaptive tests estimate a person's ability by choosing questions that are especially informative for that person. The challenge is deciding which subset to ask: question selection and ability estimation depend on one another, creating a nested optimization problem. This paper proposes a closed-form approach intended to make that selection more efficient.

The method targets ability estimation error through two mathematical properties. It reduces bias in the gradient associated with the ability parameter while keeping the Hessian stable. In plain language, it tries to improve the direction of the estimation updates without making their local behavior unstable. This formulation supports a simple greedy question-selection algorithm. It also provides a way to quantify how behavioral perturbations affect the resulting ability estimate.

On large educational datasets, the authors report that their approach needs 10% fewer questions than state-of-the-art methods at the same estimation accuracy. The practical contribution is therefore a shorter assessment for a comparable estimate, together with a mathematical framework for studying how response behavior influences reliability.
neurips-2025-a-closed-form-solution-for-.tldr: A closed-form question-selection method reduces adaptive-test length by 10% in reported experiments while preserving ability-estimation accuracy.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning can benefit from remembering a long history, especially when current observations do not fully describe the situation. However, always using a large fixed history can introduce redundant information and hinder exploration. This paper treats the amount of history available to a policy as something to adapt during learning.

A central agent adjusts context length using temporal gradient analysis. The framework also gives this agent a compact representation of what the decentralized agents have experienced. It uses a Fourier-based operation that retains low-frequency information, extracting broad temporal trends while filtering redundant detail. The two components work together: one decides how much context to use, while the other makes the information guiding that decision more efficient.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on long-term dependency tasks spanning PettingZoo, MiniGrid, Google Research Football, and SMACv2. These findings support adaptive context selection as a useful alternative to a fixed large context in the evaluated settings. The proposed exploration mechanism is intended to facilitate convergence toward global optima; the abstract does not present this as an unconditional convergence guarantee.
neurips-2025-adaptive-context-length-opt.tldr: A central agent adaptively selects history length using temporal gradients and Fourier-filtered trends, improving reported multi-agent learning performance.

paragraphs: Generating several images with matching style is difficult when style is specified only through text. Earlier alignment methods largely target U-Net diffusion architectures, making them less suitable for diffusion transformers such as Flux. AlignedGen introduces a training-free method designed specifically to coordinate style across images generated by these transformer models.

The method combines Shifted Position Embedding with Advanced Attention Sharing. The position component assigns non-overlapping position indices to alleviate the loss of text control observed when earlier approaches are applied to diffusion transformers. The attention component contains three specialized techniques for improving style alignment. Together, they address the need to share stylistic information while retaining the ability to direct each image through its text description.

AlignedGen also includes an efficient procedure for extracting query, key, and value features, allowing external images to serve as style references. Experiments show improved consistency across generated images while maintaining favorable text controllability. The contribution is therefore both architectural compatibility and practical control: coordinated visual style can be introduced into diffusion transformers without additional training.
neurips-2025-alignedgen-aligning-style-a.tldr: AlignedGen coordinates image style in diffusion transformers without training, while preserving text control and supporting external style references.

paragraphs: Multimodal alignment requires models to distinguish matching pairs from mismatched ones. Some mismatches are obvious, while others differ from a correct match by only a small detail. This paper argues that treating all negative pairs alike overlooks useful information in these ambiguous cases, and introduces Boundary-aware Curriculum with Local Attention, or BACL.

BACL combines two modules. A negative sampler gradually increases difficulty, organizing learning around progressively more challenging mismatches. A contrastive local attention loss emphasizes where the mismatch occurs. This couples the choice of training examples with a signal about the specific difference the model should notice. The authors describe both components as fully differentiable and compatible with off-the-shelf dual encoders.

The theoretical analysis predicts an error rate of approximately 1/n, up to logarithmic factors. Empirically, the authors report improvements of up to 32% in recall at rank one over CLIP and state-of-the-art results on four large benchmarks, without additional labels. These results support using subtle mismatches as structured learning signals rather than giving every negative pair the same treatment.
neurips-2025-aligning-by-misaligning-bou.tldr: BACL improves multimodal alignment by gradually introducing harder mismatches and directing attention to the details that make them incorrect.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models generate discrete sequences by gradually revealing hidden tokens. With only two token states, hidden or revealed, consecutive sampling steps can receive exactly the same sequence. The paper identifies this repeated processing as a source of redundant computation and proposes Partial masking, called Prime, to make the generation process more fine-grained.

Prime introduces intermediate token states between fully masked and fully visible. The model can therefore make predictions from partial information instead of waiting for a token to become completely available. The authors derive a variational training objective and add an architectural design that accepts these intermediate inputs. This changes both what the model observes during generation and how it learns to remove uncertainty.

On OpenWebText, Prime achieves perplexity of 15.36, compared with 21.52 for previous masked diffusion models, 17.54 for autoregressive models, and 17.58 for hybrid variants. It does so without an autoregressive formulation. Image results include FID scores of 3.26 on CIFAR-10 and 6.98 on ImageNet-32, which the authors describe as competitive with leading continuous generative models.
neurips-2025-beyond-masked-and-unmasked-.tldr: Prime gives diffusion tokens partially visible states, enabling finer-grained generation and strong reported text and image results.

paragraphs: Robot manipulation needs both contextual reasoning and fast control. Existing dual-system approaches often assign these jobs to separate models, which limits how directly the action system can use a pretrained vision-language model's knowledge. Fast-in-Slow places the fast execution module inside the slower reasoning model through partial parameter sharing.

The two systems retain different responsibilities. They receive different combinations of input modalities and operate at asynchronous frequencies, allowing action generation to proceed faster than high-level reasoning. A dual-aware co-training strategy develops the execution system's action capabilities while preserving the reasoning system's contextual understanding. That understanding supplies stable latent conditions to guide the faster component within the unified model.

The authors report average success-rate improvements of 8% in simulation and 11% on real-world tasks over previous state-of-the-art methods. They also report a control frequency of 117.7 Hz with the action chunk set to eight. These results show that, in the evaluated tasks and configuration, sharing part of the model can support both effective manipulation and high-frequency execution.
neurips-2025-fast-in-slow-a-dual-system-.tldr: Fast-in-Slow partially shares parameters between robotic reasoning and execution, improving reported task success while enabling high-frequency control.

paragraphs: Choosing pretraining data for a vision-language model involves deciding which examples will help on later tasks. Filter Like You Test, or FLYT, learns that judgment from downstream task training sets. It trains a scoring model using their gradient signals, so the importance assigned to an example's features reflects evidence about downstream usefulness.

Mixing-FLYT extends this idea by treating scores from different scoring methods as input features and learning how to combine them. FLYT produces a probability distribution over examples, which the authors use through Soft Cap Sampling. This sampling procedure builds the filtered dataset while applying a repetition penalty, reducing the risk that high-probability examples become overrepresented.

On the DataComp medium filtering benchmark, the approach reaches 40.1% ImageNet zero-shot accuracy. The authors report an absolute improvement of 2% over previous results and 5.5% over previous results using only public resources. Across 38 DataComp evaluation tasks, average performance reaches 37.7%, exceeding earlier public-resource approaches by 0.4%. The findings show how learning data-selection rules can improve pretraining outcomes.
neurips-2025-filter-like-you-test-data-d.tldr: FLYT learns which pretraining examples help downstream tasks and samples them with repetition control, improving reported CLIP benchmark performance.

paragraphs: A straight line between two high-dimensional data points may pass through regions that do not resemble the data. When data follows a curved manifold, meaningful shortest paths depend on a distance rule that changes with location. This paper derives such Riemannian metrics from pretrained energy-based models, which assign lower energy to higher-density regions.

The authors introduce two metrics that turn an energy model into a description of local geometry. Those metrics support the computation of geodesics: shortest paths measured according to the learned geometry. The purpose is to let the data distribution influence the route between points, rather than relying only on ordinary distances in the surrounding space.

Evaluation covers synthetic data with known density, rotated character images, and high-resolution natural images represented in a pretrained VAE's latent space. The resulting paths stay closer to the data manifold and show less curvature distortion, assessed through alignment with ground-truth trajectories. The authors report consistent improvements over established baselines, particularly in high dimensions, supporting energy models as a practical source of data-aware geometry.
neurips-2025-follow-the-energy-find-the-.tldr: Two distance metrics derived from pretrained energy models produce shortest paths that better follow the geometry of evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Contrastive examples are pairs of instances that differ only slightly but have different labels. Their appeal is that the small difference between the instances can help explain the change in label. This paper develops a theoretical framework for studying what such examples contribute to active learning, where the learner participates in obtaining training information.

The central question concerns sample complexity: how many examples are needed to learn a concept class. The framework examines how that requirement depends on the type of contrastive examples provided. This makes the choice of pairs part of the learning problem itself. A pair's value is connected to the distinction it reveals, so studying contrastive examples requires more than simply counting two labeled instances.

The authors illustrate their results using geometric concept classes and Boolean function classes. They also identify a connection with the classical model of self-directed learning. The contribution is a formal basis for comparing ways of supplying contrastive information and understanding their effect on learning requirements, rather than a claim that every kind of contrastive pair always improves learning.
neurips-2025-formal-models-of-active-lea.tldr: A theoretical framework studies how different contrastive example choices affect active-learning sample complexity and connects them to self-directed learning.

paragraphs: Adding 3D human motion to language-based foundation models presents two connected challenges. Learning the new modality can weaken existing language knowledge, and pose representations must work with autoregressive generation across different tasks. HMVLM addresses both within a unified human motion, vision, and language framework.

The model uses a mixture of low-rank adaptation experts. A gating network selects how to allocate expert weights according to the input prompt, allowing multiple tasks to be fine-tuned together. A special zero expert preserves pretrained parameters for general language tasks, helping mitigate catastrophic forgetting. For motion representation, the method divides body joints into groups and tokenizes them by body part, increasing the spatial resolution available in the pose representation.

Experiments show that HMVLM alleviates knowledge forgetting during instruction tuning and performs strongly across diverse human-motion tasks. The stated result is a reduction in forgetting, rather than its complete elimination. The broader contribution is a coordinated design in which prompt-dependent adaptation and more detailed pose tokens support the integration of motion capabilities with existing linguistic knowledge.
neurips-2025-hmvlm-human-motion-vision-l.tldr: HMVLM combines prompt-routed adaptation experts and body-part pose tokens to learn motion tasks while reducing language-knowledge forgetting.

paragraphs: Placing an object into an image of a person requires more than making its edges blend into the background. The person's pose must support a plausible interaction, while both the object and person retain consistent appearances. HOComp addresses this interaction-aware composition problem through coordinated pose guidance and appearance preservation.

Its pose component uses multimodal large language models to identify the interaction region and type. These decisions provide coarse-to-fine guidance, supplemented by human pose landmarks that track action changes and constrain finer details. Its appearance component combines shape-aware attention modulation with losses for multi-view appearance and background consistency. These mechanisms aim to preserve the object's shape and texture while faithfully reproducing the background person.

The authors also introduce IHOC, a dataset for interaction-aware human-object composition. Experiments on that dataset show more harmonious interactions and consistent appearances, with qualitative and quantitative improvements over relevant methods. The findings support treating human pose and visual identity as linked requirements of composition, rather than assessing an inserted object solely by how naturally it blends into a selected region.
neurips-2025-hocomp-interaction-aware-hu.tldr: HOComp combines interaction-specific pose guidance and appearance preservation to create more coherent human-object image compositions.

paragraphs: Searching for a 3D scene through text is difficult when the initial description leaves out relevant information. Existing retrieval approaches often implicitly assume a complete query. IDeal instead makes retrieval interactive, using successive questions and answers to improve the correspondence between the description and candidate scenes.

Its Interactive Retrieval Refinement framework includes a questioner, an answerer, and a retriever. Questions can probe scene details or encourage broader exploration. As answers accumulate, the retriever combines information at both the feature and semantic levels to refine scene rankings. This turns the query into an evolving source of evidence rather than a fixed description used only once.

The authors also introduce Interaction Adaptation Tuning to address differences between initial queries and text produced during interaction. It uses contrastive domain adaptation while addressing discriminability and diversity risks in augmented text features. Experiments on three datasets show that IDeal outperforms the compared approaches. The results support jointly designing the interaction process and retriever adaptation, so additional dialogue can translate into more precise scene retrieval.
neurips-2025-interactive-cross-modal-lea.tldr: IDeal improves text-to-3D-scene retrieval through iterative questioning, information fusion, and adaptation to conversational descriptions.

paragraphs: Graph models combine node attributes with connections between nodes, but their predictions can be difficult to interpret. Additive graph models make individual feature contributions more explicit, yet the prior GNAN approach has substantial parameter demands and overlooks local aggregation. G-NAMRFF aims to preserve that interpretability while improving efficiency and the use of graph structure.

Each node representation is expressed as a sum of feature-specific contributions. These contributions are modeled through a Gaussian process with a kernel that incorporates both features and graph information. The kernel combines a radial basis function with structure induced by the graph Laplacian and a learnable finite impulse response filter. Random Fourier features approximate this kernel, producing a Bayesian formulation learned with a single-layer neural network.

The authors report 168 times fewer parameters than GNAN. Despite its smaller size, G-NAMRFF matches or exceeds state-of-the-art GNNs and GNAN on evaluated node and graph classification tasks. Its additive construction also provides real-time interpretability. The results suggest that explicit feature contributions and graph-aware modeling can coexist with compact representations and competitive classification performance.
neurips-2025-interpretable-and-parameter.tldr: G-NAMRFF combines interpretable feature contributions with graph-aware kernels, reporting competitive accuracy with 168 times fewer parameters than GNAN.

paragraphs: Imitating expert behavior in a multi-agent game raises a strategic question: will the learned policies still form an equilibrium? This paper characterizes the expert-data requirements for learning a Nash equilibrium in Markov games. It identifies a quantity called the single policy deviation concentrability coefficient as unavoidable when learning cannot interact with the expert.

The authors provide a behavioral-cloning upper bound involving this coefficient and show that behavioral cloning has substantial regret when the coefficient is large. This motivates algorithms that can query an expert. MAIL-BRO also uses a best-response oracle, which supplies information about strategic responses. MURMAIL removes the need for that oracle, exchanging this simpler access requirement for a higher expert-query cost.

MAIL-BRO learns an ε-Nash equilibrium using O(ε⁻⁴) expert and oracle queries. MURMAIL has expert-query complexity O(ε⁻⁸). These rates expose a concrete tradeoff between access to a best-response oracle and the amount of expert interaction required. Numerical evidence supports the theoretical findings, connecting the analysis of imitation's difficulties with algorithms designed to overcome them.
neurips-2025-learning-equilibria-from-da.tldr: The paper characterizes equilibrium-learning requirements and introduces two expert-query algorithms with different oracle access and query-complexity tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Segmenting 3D medical images requires attention to local structures and the broader volume containing them. Processing these long inputs efficiently becomes harder when imaging modalities and data quality vary. HoME introduces a hierarchical mixture-of-experts routing layer built on the Mamba selective state space model to address this combination of requirements.

The routing process has two levels. First, a soft mixture-of-experts layer divides input sequences into local groups and sends tokens to specialized experts within each group. These experts extract localized features. A second, global layer then combines the group outputs, allowing information to move across groups and refining the wider context. The hierarchy explicitly connects local processing with global information fusion.

The authors report improved generalizability and segmentation performance, surpassing state-of-the-art results on datasets covering three widely used 3D medical imaging modalities and varying data quality. These findings support adaptive expert routing as a way to strengthen Mamba's sequential modeling for volumetric segmentation. The central contribution is the two-stage organization of expertise, which gives local specialization and global refinement distinct roles.
neurips-2025-mamba-goes-home-hierarchica.tldr: HoME adds local and global expert routing to Mamba, improving reported 3D medical-image segmentation across modalities and data qualities.

paragraphs: Training-data errors, corruption, and poisoning can change the model produced by learning. MIBP-Cert studies these effects through certification: it computes deterministic bounds intended to cover every outcome allowed by a specified perturbation model. The goal is to provide provable statements about training robustness, beyond observing how a defense performs against selected corruptions.

The method formulates the problem using mixed-integer bilinear programming. It bounds the model parameters that can be reached when training data is perturbed or manipulated. Covering those possible parameters makes it possible to reason about the resulting model outcomes. Because solving this optimization directly is difficult, the authors introduce a relaxation that bounds each training step while retaining soundness.

The paper demonstrates applicability to continuous and discrete data and to several threat models, including complex cases previously out of reach. The significance of the relaxation is that computational simplification does not abandon the guarantee that permitted outcomes are covered. The resulting robustness claims are tied to the perturbations represented by the chosen threat model and the bounds computed for them.
neurips-2025-mibp-cert-certified-trainin.tldr: MIBP-Cert soundly bounds models reachable under specified training-data perturbations using mixed-integer bilinear optimization and tractable relaxations.

paragraphs: This paper studies a stochastic bandit problem in which a learner repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards. Here, multimodal describes the shape of the expected reward function: it has at most m modes, or peaks. The setting assumes independent and identically distributed rewards, and the upper bound on the number of modes is part of the problem's structure.

The main contribution is a computationally tractable algorithm for solving the Graves-Lai optimization problem in this setting. That optimization is a key step in making asymptotically optimal bandit algorithms implementable. The distinction matters because a theoretical prescription for optimal behavior is more useful when the computation it requires can actually be performed.

The authors describe their solver as the first known tractable method for this problem. Its stated consequence is to enable asymptotically optimal algorithms for the specified multimodal bandit setting. This is a long-run optimality result, rather than a statement that every early decision is optimal. The contribution connects a structured reward assumption with a computational route to implementing the corresponding optimal learning behavior.
neurips-2025-multimodal-bandits-regret-l.tldr: A tractable Graves-Lai solver enables asymptotically optimal bandit algorithms when expected rewards have at most m modes.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning for treatment planning must avoid recommendations unsupported by clinical data. The paper argues that constraining individual actions is insufficient because a sequence of seemingly acceptable actions can still lead to unsupported patient states. OGSRL addresses both action choices and their downstream trajectories within a model-based learning framework.

Its first constraint is an out-of-distribution guardian that restricts optimization to clinically validated regions, using the patient's full state history. Its second is a safety cost based on medical knowledge about physiological boundaries. This additional constraint matters because appearing in the training data does not itself make an intervention safe. The theoretical guarantees apply to policies satisfying these constraints: they stay within the specified safe, reliable regions and approach the best policy supported by the data.

On the MIMIC-III sepsis dataset, the authors report better handling of out-of-distribution behavior than baselines, a 78% reduction in mortality estimates, and a 51% reward increase relative to clinician decisions. These are results from the reported offline evaluation; the mortality finding concerns estimates, rather than an observed reduction from deploying the policy in patient care.
neurips-2025-offline-guarded-safe-reinfo.tldr: OGSRL constrains treatment-policy trajectories and physiological safety, with conditional guarantees and improved estimated outcomes in an offline sepsis evaluation.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly chooses among uncertain options, but average reward may not capture every aspect of risk that matters. This paper considers multiple risk measures when rewards are heavy-tailed. It develops a distributional framework that can account for several properties of reward distributions instead of centering the decision on a single objective.

The technical foundation is a set of new deviation inequalities for the 1-Wasserstein distance, a measure of difference between distributions. These inequalities produce confidence intervals for Lipschitz risk measures. The resulting distributional lower-confidence-bound algorithm, DistLCB, achieves asymptotic optimality. Its analysis includes lower bounds that explicitly depend on the gaps separating suboptimal choices from better ones.

The authors extend DistLCB to multiple risk objectives, enabling Pareto-optimal solutions that balance different distributional concerns. They also derive both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds for this setting. Synthetic and real-world experiments support the methods' effectiveness. Together, the results connect uncertainty about entire reward distributions with theoretically analyzed decisions involving more than one notion of risk.
neurips-2025-pareto-optimal-risk-agnosti.tldr: DistLCB uses distributional confidence bounds to learn under heavy-tailed rewards and balance multiple risk objectives with Pareto-optimal solutions.

paragraphs: High-dynamic-range cameras capture brightness differences and details that conventional image inputs cannot represent as easily. Yet embedded object detectors are usually trained on low-dynamic-range images, creating a mismatch when they receive high-bit-depth HDR data. This paper proposes a tone-mapping pipeline that converts HDR RAW inputs into the LDR sRGB representation expected by detection networks.

The conversion is optimized end to end with the downstream task. Neural photometric calibration regularizes the dynamic range, while a scaling-invariant local tone-mapping module preserves image details. The architecture also supports performance-transfer fine-tuning, allowing an existing LDR model to adapt efficiently to HDR RAW inputs. This ties image conversion to detection needs rather than treating it as a separate preprocessing objective.

In challenging automotive HDR scenes, the authors report better performance than traditional tone-mapping algorithms and advanced AI image-signal-processing methods. They also demonstrate real-time processing of 4K high-bit-depth HDR inputs on Nvidia Jetson. The findings combine detection effectiveness with an embedded deployment result, showing that task-optimized HDR conversion can operate at the reported resolution in real time.
neurips-2025-real-time-scene-adaptive-to.tldr: Task-optimized neural tone mapping improves automotive HDR object detection and processes 4K high-bit-depth inputs in real time on Jetson.

paragraphs: Deep forecasting models can capture complicated temporal patterns, but they can also overfit noise and anomalies. Standard mean squared error training gives every timestep a role in optimization, including points that may not support generalizable learning. This paper proposes selecting which timesteps contribute to the loss rather than treating all of them equally.

The selection uses two masks with different jobs. An uncertainty mask relies on residual entropy to filter uncertain timesteps. An anomaly mask uses residual lower-bound estimation to exclude anomalous ones. The remaining subset supplies the mean squared error used for optimization. This changes the learning signal so that the forecasting model focuses on timesteps judged more useful for generalization.

Across eight real-world datasets, selective learning improves the predictive performance of typical state-of-the-art deep forecasting models. The authors report mean squared error reductions of 37.4% for Informer, 8.4% for TimesNet, and 6.5% for iTransformer. These findings support the idea that controlling which observations influence optimization can improve existing forecasting models, with gains that vary across the evaluated architectures.
neurips-2025-selective-learning-for-deep.tldr: Selective learning filters uncertain and anomalous timesteps from the training loss, improving reported accuracy across several deep forecasting models.

paragraphs: Fairness assessments often compare one estimated metric with a fixed threshold, overlooking how much uncertainty comes from limited data. This becomes especially problematic for intersectional groups, where combinations of demographic attributes can leave very few observations per group. The paper introduces a statistical testing framework that adapts to subgroup size.

For sufficiently large groups, the authors prove a central-limit result for statistical parity difference. This yields analytic confidence intervals and a Wald test with type-I error controlled at level α. For small groups, they derive a Bayesian Dirichlet–multinomial estimator and obtain credible intervals through Monte Carlo computation. The abstract states that these intervals are calibrated for any sample size and converge naturally toward Wald intervals as data grows.

Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate interpretable fairness decisions across different levels of data availability and intersectionality. The contribution is a unified way to incorporate estimation uncertainty while changing the statistical machinery to suit the subgroup size. It replaces a bare point-estimate comparison with an assessment whose evidence reflects how much data supports the fairness measurement.
neurips-2025-size-adaptive-hypothesis-te.tldr: A size-adaptive fairness framework combines large-sample hypothesis tests with Bayesian estimation for small intersectional groups.

paragraphs: Support Vector Generation turns a frozen language model into a classifier for zero-shot and few-shot tasks without fine-tuning its parameters. Instead of making each classification through prompting alone, it uses the model's embedding space to construct a kernel-based decision rule. The resulting prediction depends on explicit natural-language support sentences.

The framework combines Metropolis–Hastings sampling with support vector machine optimization in the embedding-induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Each decision uses a weighted combination of at most 32 sentences, which the authors present as faithful rationales. Their analysis proves minimization of empirical hinge loss within the span of those supports and gives a generalization bound independent of language-model size.

On multiple GLUE tasks, SVG matches or exceeds prompting-based zero-shot baselines in accuracy. Its CPU-only implementation completes the classifier's training procedure in under three minutes per task and retains competitive inference speed, without GPU acceleration or language-model fine-tuning. The results suggest a practical route to classification that exposes its supporting sentences while keeping the underlying language model fixed.
neurips-2025-support-vector-generation-k.tldr: SVG builds efficient classifiers from frozen language-model embeddings, grounding each decision in at most 32 explicit support sentences.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction methods often face a choice between learning from many clean images and optimizing a network separately for each degraded observation. Deep Image Prior takes the latter route, but can overfit noise and require substantial computation. UGoDIT uses a small collection of degraded measurements to learn reusable weights without requiring clean ground-truth images.

During training, the method optimizes a shared encoder and M separate, disentangled decoders for the M available measurement vectors. At test time, it reconstructs an unseen degraded image using a Deep Image Prior network. Some parameters are fixed to the learned weights, while the remaining parameters are optimized to make the reconstruction consistent with the measurement. This combines transferable information with adaptation to the individual reconstruction problem.

Evaluations cover multi-coil MRI, super-resolution, and nonlinear deblurring. Compared with recent standalone Deep Image Prior methods, UGoDIT converges faster and improves reconstruction quality. The authors also report performance competitive with state-of-the-art diffusion-based and supervised approaches. These results concern a low-data setting where only a very small set of subsampled measurements is available for training.
neurips-2025-ugodit-unsupervised-group-d.tldr: UGoDIT learns transferable reconstruction weights from a few degraded measurements, accelerating Deep Image Prior reconstruction and improving reported image quality.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional vector graphics summarize an object's essential structure in a compact representation. This makes them useful for tasks such as shape retrieval, conceptual design, and virtual-reality interaction. However, existing generation approaches can take substantial time and produce sketches whose appearance is inconsistent across viewpoints. ViewCraft3D addresses both processing cost and view consistency.

The method uses 3D priors and begins by analyzing the object. A geometric extraction algorithm then fits vector graphics to the object's underlying structure. A subsequent refinement stage improves visual quality while maintaining consistency between views. The sequence gives structural extraction and visual refinement separate roles, with the three-dimensional object providing the basis for the generated sketch.

The authors report better qualitative and quantitative results than previous methods, together with substantially reduced computational overhead. The generated sketches preserve essential characteristics of the original objects and remain consistent when viewed from different directions. These findings support using 3D structural information throughout generation, so the compact output can represent the object coherently across views while requiring less computation than the compared approaches.
neurips-2025-viewcraft3d-high-fidelity-a.tldr: ViewCraft3D uses object geometry and view-consistent refinement to produce coherent 3D vector sketches with lower reported computational overhead.
